title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER XXXVII
enhanced_title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER XXXVII - Contemplations of Refused Proposals and Lady Catherine's Condescension
author: Jane Austen
description: Elizabeth Bennet reflects upon Mr. Darcy's letter and the implications of his revelations while enduring Lady Catherine de Bourgh's overbearing attentions during her final week at Rosings Park.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Chapter XXXVII marks the period of introspection following Darcy's proposal and letter. Elizabeth's internal struggle is vividly portrayed as she oscillates between anger at his initial address and remorse for her own unjustified accusations. This psychological tension represents Austen's mastery in depicting the complexity of first impressions and self-knowledge, and the chapter's quiet domestic setting throws that inner turbulence into sharp relief.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Reflection
must be reserved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she gave
way to it as the greatest relief; and not a day went by without a
solitary walk, in which she might indulge in all the delight of
unpleasant recollections.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lady Catherine de Bourgh serves as a foil to Elizabeth, embodying aristocratic pretension and the rigid class structure that Darcy initially embraced. Her condescending offer to extend the visit and her unsolicited advice about travel arrangements underscore the patronizing attitude Elizabeth would have faced had she accepted Darcy's proposal. The irony is sharpest when Elizabeth privately reflects that she might by this time have been presented to Lady Catherine as her future niece, and silently imagines her Ladyship's indignation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth could not see Lady Catherine without recollecting that, had
she chosen it, she might by this time have been presented to her as her
future niece; nor could she think, without a smile, of what her
Ladyship’s indignation would have been.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter underscores the theme of female vulnerability in Georgian society, particularly through Lady Catherine's obsessive concern with proper escorts for young women travelling alone. Her insistence that young women should always be properly guarded and attended, according to their situation in life, ironically foreshadows the very scandal involving Wickham and Georgiana that Elizabeth has just learned about through Darcy's letter. This anxiety about female propriety masks deeper anxieties about family honour and the precarious position of women dependent on male protection and social reputation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Young women should always be properly
guarded and attended, according to their situation in life.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's solitary walks become a metaphor for the isolation necessary for genuine reflection. The pastoral setting of Rosings Park, normally associated with aristocratic leisure, is transformed into the space where Elizabeth confronts uncomfortable truths about her family's conduct and her own prejudiced judgments. Austen signals this inward turn with the observation that reflection must be reserved for solitary hours, marking the walks as the novel's primary site of psychological reckoning in this chapter.

Mr. Collins's continued obsequiousness toward Lady Catherine demonstrates the stifling nature of social climbing and deference to rank. His willingness to interpret the ordinary departure of guests as a 'melancholy scene' illustrates the performative nature of class relationships among those aspiring to gentility. Having been in waiting near the lodges to make his parting obeisance, Collins embodies the comic extreme of a social order that Elizabeth, by contrast, navigates with ironic detachment.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Mr. Collins having
been in waiting near the lodges, to make them his parting obeisance, was
able to bring home the pleasing intelligence of their appearing in very
good health, and in as tolerable spirits as could be expected, after the
melancholy scene so lately gone through at Rosings.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's realization of her family's hopeless impropriety—particularly her father's indulgent neglect and her mother's vulgarity—represents a painful coming-of-age moment. Austen renders this with unusual directness: the defects of her family are described as hopeless of remedy, a verdict that strips away any consoling illusion. This recognition that family cannot be reformed or escaped adds a tragic dimension to the comedy of manners, and it is the weight of this knowledge that makes Elizabeth's cheerfulness almost impossible to maintain.

The chapter concludes with Elizabeth's heightened concern for Jane, demonstrating that Darcy's revelations have not merely affected Elizabeth personally but have deepened her empathy for her sister's loss. The restoration of Bingley's good character in Elizabeth's eyes makes Jane's deprivation feel all the more poignant, and Austen frames this grief in terms of what might have been: a situation so desirable in every respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness. The expansion of concern from self to sister reflects Elizabeth's capacity for love and loyalty even amid her own emotional turmoil.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
How
grievous then was the thought that, of a situation so desirable in every
respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness, Jane had
been deprived, by the folly and indecorum of her own family!

quote_entries.quote: Mr. Darcy's letter she was in a fair way of soon knowing by heart. She studied every sentence; and her feelings towards its writer were at times widely different.

When she remembered the style of his address, she was still full of indignation: but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and upbraided him, her anger was turned against herself; and his disappointed feelings became the object of compassion.

summary: Chapter XXXVII of Pride and Prejudice depicts Elizabeth Bennet's final days at Rosings Park, characterized by intense introspection regarding Mr. Darcy's letter and revelations. While enduring Lady Catherine de Bourgh's overbearing attention and unwanted advice, Elizabeth processes her conflicting emotions about Darcy's proposal and her family's conduct. The chapter juxtaposes external social performance with internal psychological struggle, as Elizabeth recognizes her own prejudiced judgments and her family's irremediable vulgarity. Through solitary walks and private reflection, she arrives at a painful maturity, accepting her family's flaws while recognizing the genuine nature of Jane's lost happiness with Bingley. Lady Catherine's condescending control and Mr. Collins's obsequiousness provide comic counterpoints to Elizabeth's serious self-examination.
